entry.title: Is our information ecosystem still robust? Notes from a parliamentary hearing
entry.summary: Is our information ecosystem still robust? Notes from a parliamentary hearing
entry.content:
On 20 October, my ORM colleague Antonin Descampe and I had the opportunity to testify before the Media Committee of the Parliament of the Wallonia-Brussels Federation. It is an unusual exercise: you have to sum up years of research in a short time and, above all, move from diagnosis to concrete proposals. Here are the main points we presented.

Our starting point fits in one sentence: public-interest news has almost no viable business model left in French-speaking Belgium, even though a robust information ecosystem is more necessary than ever for democracy. In other words, what looks like an economic crisis for the sector is turning into a democratic one.

A small market under pressure

The first problem is structural. Over the past thirty years, successive technological waves (the web, search engines, social media, mobile, and now AI) have placed infomediaries between news organisations and their audiences. These intermediaries capture attention and, with it, advertising revenue. In Belgium, 58.8% of digital advertising investment goes to international platforms (UMA, 2026). What remains must be shared among publishers in a market that, unlike France or the United States, is too small for a few titles to thrive on subscriptions: only 14% of Belgians pay for online news (Picone, 2026).

On top of this comes an unprecedented wave of concentration. Since the Rossel–IPM merger, approved with conditions on 3 July 2026, all six French-language daily newspapers are published or co-published by a single group, which amounts to 94% of the daily print press according to RSF. The landscape remains diverse if you look further (the mapping carried out by Clémence Petit and Olivier Standaert for the ORM and CRISP counts 118 periodicals and around sixty digital-native outlets), but these are often non-profit, volunteer-run or niche organisations whose survival is far from guaranteed.

Finally, we should not forget that producing news takes media groups, but also journalists. Their working conditions are deteriorating: a large share of freelancers (between 25% and 50%, depending on the estimate), many of whom work for a single outlet; an income gap of around 30% compared with salaried staff; and 71.5% who report a heavier workload in recent years (AJP, 2023; Labourie, 2024).

Audiences turning away and the growth of FIMI

On the audience side, the trends are well known but worth recalling. In Belgium, 41% of people get their news through social media (+4 points this year, a figure that keeps rising), compared with 49% through television and 18% through print newspapers (both figures falling year after year). Above all, 42% of French-speaking Belgians sometimes or often avoid the news, and only 28% trust it most of the time (Digital News Report, 2026).

These figures will come as no surprise to anyone who follows these issues, but their persistence should be more of a cause for concern. This is all the more true given the growing development of what European institutions call FIMI (Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference): coordinated and intentional operations through which foreign actors attempt to manipulate a country’s information space in order to influence democratic processes, notably elections (the EEAS documents more than 540 incidents of this type in 2025, spread across more than 10,500 different social media channels and websites (EEAS, 2026)).

AI as an accelerator

As my colleague Antonin, who specialises in this question, points out: AI does not create these weaknesses, it accelerates them. Three mechanisms seem particularly important to us:

  • Greater technological dependence. The large American tech companies, which already controlled the distribution of news, now also control a growing share of the means of producing it (Simon, 2022). The printing presses were in Nivelles; the servers are in the United States.
  • Media becoming invisible. Journalistic content becomes a raw material, absorbed and rephrased by AI assistants, then detached from its source. 28% of people who see an AI summary rarely or never click through to the sources (Simon, Nielsen & Fletcher, 2025), while 45% of these assistants' answers about the news contain at least one significant issue (EBU & BBC, 2025).
  • The industrialisation of disinformation. It is now possible to produce anything and deliver it to anyone. The risk is not only that people believe what is false, but also that they stop believing what is true: this is known as the "liar's dividend". I see it as an extension of what I described, in an earlier post, as a form of automated doubt.

What can be done?

We argued for a robust and resilient local information ecosystem, suited to the "small market" of French-speaking Belgium. It is an economic question, but not only that. Concretely, we put forward several proposals:

  1. Build an evidence base. Consolidated data on journalists' employment, status and income, or on the effectiveness of public support, are sorely lacking. A governance tool for public media policy would make it possible to track how these evolve.
  2. Rethink (and increase) funding, with support differentiated between small organisations and large groups, and a responsible approach to the decline of print.
  3. Stabilise revenues, by making subscriptions easier and redirecting public-sector advertising towards local players.
  4. Encourage "coopetition": pool certain infrastructure (AI tools, distribution platforms) and negotiate collectively with AI companies. Public service media could act as robustness infrastructure rather than as a mere competitor.
  5. Protect the profession, in particular by tackling bogus self-employment, making public support conditional on employment standards, and changing how journalists' copyright income is taxed.
  6. Educate audiences in media and algorithmic literacy.
  7. Genuinely enforce the European framework (EMFA, DSA, DMA, AI Act). Its impact will depend less on its adoption than on the investigative powers and data access that come with its implementation.

None of these measures will be enough on its own, and they fall under different levels of government (the Wallonia-Brussels Federation, the Regions, the federal state, the European Union). This may be the main difficulty (as is often the case in Belgium): the problem is systemic, while the levers are scattered.

What next?

This is not the first time researchers have raised the alarm on these issues, and it will not be the last. But we feel that this moment is different: press concentration, the announced end of certain subsidies and the massive arrival of AI in the news production chain are all happening within a very short time.

This is also why we are preparing, at the ORM, a public website that will bring together the results of our surveys on news practices, distrust of the media, newsroom diversity and the mapping of the press in French-speaking Belgium. I will come back to it here soon.

In short: a robust information ecosystem does not maintain itself; it has to be built, and that requires urgent and coordinated public action.

The slides from the hearing and the full list of references are available on request.

Main references: Digital News Report 2026 (Reuters Institute); Petit & Standaert, Cartographie des médias d'information en Belgique francophone (CRISP, 2025); RSF (2026); UMA, via X. Degraux (2026); EBU & BBC, News Integrity in AI Assistants (2025); Simon, Nielsen & Fletcher, Generative AI and News Report (2025).

entry.title: AI and the dispersion of expertise
entry.summary: How generative tools redistribute epistemic authority.
entry.content:
One of the issues raised by the development of conversational AIs - which might more accurately be described as centralized banks of knowledge and expertise - is that they contradict the mechanism of expertise dispersion within society.

Today, if you have a legal problem, you can consult a lawyer who has spent many years developing a specific expertise and who will help you resolve the issue.

Since there is more than one lawyer offering such services, on the one hand, you have a choice among a diversity of individuals and therefore of areas of expertise. But more importantly, from a sociological perspective, legal expertise is dispersed throughout society (even though some law firms do centralize certain specializations and acquire dominant positions in the legal expertise market).

Sociologically, legal expertise exists redundantly within society through the practice of a multitude of lawyers, judges, legal assistants, and jurists. This is also true for other types of expertise (economic, accounting, medical, etc.).

This dispersion is one of the foundations of how our societies function, both organizationally and democratically. This mechanism of expertise dispersion (or specialization of individuals) is also often at the heart of how we build our social identities (we define ourselves as lawyers, nurses, teachers, nutritionists, travel agents, etc.). It also plays a central role in how we organize the symbolic and economic hierarchies that structure society.

The dispersion of expertise is a core organizational principle of our societies and of our lives as individuals.

The promise of centralized banks of knowledge and expertise (aka conversational AIs) is to offer a digital one-stop shop (currently owned by a private company often based in California) for the consultation of all kinds of expertise, by everyone, in all societies. An expertise that, moreover, instantly adapts to our individual specificities based on previously collected data about our preferences, behaviors, and opinions.

If the use of centralized knowledge and expertise banks were to become widespread, our societies could be profoundly reconfigured, since the principle of centralization of expertise that underpins them is opposed to the principle of dispersion that currently governs our collective functioning.

Note: This text is an atomated translation of the French version of the text found here.

entry.title: Automation as a Cue of Factitiousness
entry.summary: AI gives a first impression of factitiousness.
entry.content:
In this post, I will tell a small anecdote that happened to me this week while I was trying, together with a few friends, to (re)start exercising, and show how it illustrates a possibly rapid change in our ability to trust the information circulating in today's digital information environments.

AI and the colonization of digital environments by automated media

To pull the threads of this anecdote together, a few preliminaries are needed.

The first is that the development of conversational AI and other automatic content generation tools, and above all the very rapid spread of their use by actors with varying degrees of good faith, raises a whole series of questions and fears about the proper functioning of information environments.

One of these fears is that the web, and digital information environments more generally, are gradually filling up with slop, that is, false or low-quality information generated automatically by AI tools. It follows that having to navigate every day a digital environment saturated with slop could aggravate the information disorders already identified: disinformation, malinformation, misinformation, etc.

A second dimension of this fear is that, in a digital information environment where content is increasingly produced by what my colleagues Jerry Jacques and Antonin Descampe call "automated media", it will become more and more difficult to assess both the reliability of sources and the factitiousness of the content we are confronted with.

With the generalization of automated media, the very notions of author and source are transformed. The growing automation of digital media content production could therefore not only intensify information disorders but, above all (and this is, I think, what my anecdote from this week will show), reshape our relationship to information deemed reliable or of good quality.

To navigate a digital environment filled with "slop", we must (or at least should) constantly ask ourselves the following questions:

  • Was the press or scientific journal article I am reading really published in the journal I am interested in, or is it a fake copy meant to deceive me?
  • Does the email I received really come from my boss, or is it a very realistic phishing attempt imitating a message from my boss?
  • Is the sender of this Instagram message a real person, or a bot?
  • Is the answer to the question I asked Grok or Gemini actually valid, or does it rest on inaccurate information, or even on an ideologically skewed view of reality?
  • Was the gardening blog I am reading (yes, at 40 you read gardening blogs...) written by an expert on the subject, or was it generated in two minutes by an AI that says whatever comes to mind?

In short, the ongoing colonization of the digital environment by a new type of media, automated media, could well destabilize that environment's functioning as an information environment, that is, as a collective space in which we form our relationship to the world by acquiring knowledge and information that we deem reliable.

Reception and trust in information environments

The second preliminary is that the effect of a new medium and its content on society and individuals is never direct. If this effect is measurable, it is measured largely by taking into account how the people who use the medium to communicate receive its content.

If we are interested in the effect of the ongoing colonization of digital environments by automated media, it is therefore relevant to ask how the reception practices they may provoke could change.

Faced with media production, we are never passive; we are in an active interpretive stance. We try to make sense of the messages we receive and of the content we read or watch, and it is in this continuous interpretive activity (often very rapid, even unconscious) that the meaning of the content is ultimately constituted, and with it its possible "effect" on our perceptions, attitudes or activities.

We can hypothesize that in a functioning information environment it is relatively easy (whatever criteria the participating person uses) to assess the quality and reliability of both a source and a piece of information. In any case, it must be possible to know whether or not we can trust the source of the information.

In 2025, our information environment consists of a variety of sources, both physical or analog and digital: friends, parents, colleagues, teachers, books, traditional news media (press, TV, radio), blogs, social media influencers, scientific journals, professional newsletters, local newspapers, and so on.

These sources are relatively stable over time, and we have learned either that we can trust them or that they are not reliable. This operation is mainly personal and the result of an interpretive act. For example, one person may judge the RTBF news (the Belgian public broadcaster) to be extremely reliable and another may see it as a collection of lies; depending on this initial evaluation, its content will not be interpreted in the same way and will not have the same "effect" on us. This activity also has an important social dimension, however: it is, for instance, generally accepted in Belgium that the RTBF is a quality source that can be relied upon.

Once this trust has been acquired and stabilized, there is no need to re-evaluate it at each new interaction with the source. This stability of media trust is probably one of the conditions of possibility of a functioning information environment. And the existence of a functioning and relatively stable information environment is probably one of the conditions of possibility of life in democratic societies in the twenty-first century.

From this point of view, the digitization of information environments, caused by the development of the web in the 1990s and above all of Web 2.0 from 2000 to 2020, had significant consequences. New types of media sources appeared, such as encyclopedias written by non-professionals (Wikipedia), online newspapers, blogs, social media accounts, and so on. Almost all of these digital sources have in common that they are produced by non-professionals with very diverse skills, so their reliability could no longer be automatically inferred from the specialized status of their author (journalists, scientists, experts). The evaluation of source reliability thus became more central, and so, probably, did the collective processes by which trust is attributed to certain sources judged more reliable than others.

What is interesting is that we have gradually learned collectively, and it took almost 30 years, whether and how we could (or could not) trust these new sources and how they could contribute to our information mix. This process took time, is still not over, and gives rise to many debates.

With these preliminaries in place, I can come to my aborted attempt to exercise and show why it is a good example of a possible ongoing destabilization of the trust structures of digital information environments, and how this destabilization can cause very concrete problems in our everyday lives.

My (non-)participation in a trail run and a debate among friends about the factitiousness of an email

A few weeks ago, I signed up with three friends for a trail run scheduled for the end of May in a town near Brussels. Nothing out of the ordinary. The event was being organized for the first time by an experienced company, in a very professional manner. A flawless website in French and Dutch powered by Odoo, impeccable social media accounts (Facebook, Instagram and TikTok) with slick promotional videos, and so on.

Last week, surprisingly, all four of us received an email announcing that, for lack of sufficient registrations, the event was going to be cancelled and that we would therefore be contacted about refunding the registration fees. Great disappointment on our part, but above all, great surprise.

Reactions to this email within our group were very varied. For two of us, there was no doubt: this email was spam, a phishing attempt to harvest our bank details. The event was going ahead and we should keep training for it. The third, on the contrary, saw it as an authentic email and thus a simple cancellation notice, and the fourth could not decide but leaned more toward spam than toward an authentic email. So there was no way for us to agree.

The elements used to justify the claim that this email could not be considered reliable were the following:

  • The sender address was of the type "info@45698122.xxx.com". No doubt: the sender had nothing to do with the race organizer. The domain of the address was not that of the event's website, and the address was not the same as the one used in the previous emails we had received. Above all, the series of digits in the address was a sure sign that the sending was automated. A robot must have taken part in this mailing in one way or another.
  • The email contained the following sentence: "We will get back to you shortly regarding the terms of the refund of your registration." A sign of a possible scam designed to collect our bank details.
  • Finally, after checking, none of the event's other communication channels (website, Facebook, Instagram or TikTok accounts) mentioned its cancellation.

Conversely, for the third of us, there was no doubt:

  • The email was formatted with very professional Mailchimp-type software, which was consistent with the other communication tools used by the organizers.
  • It was written in perfect French and Dutch, without errors and very concisely, with no trace of approximate machine translation.
  • Above all, it asked for no direct action on our part. No link to click that would take us outside the event's known media, or that would ask us to enter our bank details somewhere.
  • Moreover, the email had clearly been sent only to people registered for the event. If it were spam, it would have meant that the hackers had access to the organizers' database, which is not impossible but still quite unlikely, and above all a great deal of energy expended by hackers for such a small event. In short, no reason to doubt its authenticity.

In the end, after five days of debate among ourselves, and tired of waiting for parallel information to appear on the event's website or social media (it never did: either the event was cancelled and they should have published the information, or their database had been corrupted and they should have informed us), we found a contact email address to write to, and a person at the organizing company did confirm that the event was cancelled. End of the suspense.

The trigger for doubt in our case was the identification of an automated process behind the sending of the email (the email address made of numbers being a cue of automation, and therefore of possible factitiousness, which we have learned to recognize). What intrigued me most was the extremely rapid and stable character of this evaluation for two of us (and afterwards for a third person outside our group whom we asked for an opinion). There was no doubt, it was spam (even though our mailboxes' spam filters had not flagged it as such). The fact that the verification work also failed to yield a result (the information was not available redundantly across the company's other media, which is yet another characteristic of digital communication that we have learned to recognize over time) was clear confirmation of factitiousness. Despite a critical effort of investigation, we could not remove the doubt that had assailed us.

I think that a year or two ago, before the acceleration in the development of automated media and their colonization of digital environments, we would not have had the almost automatic reflex of doubting the reliability of this email.

This little episode illustrates that this rapid transformation of digital information environments may have as a consequence a rapid change in our relationship to information and in our ability to distinguish reliable from unreliable digital sources. It is possible that these new automated media, more than their predecessors, complicate the activity of content reception and therefore destabilize, perhaps severely, the functioning of our information spaces by complicating the interpretive work they impose on us.

To the automation of media, there might thus correspond an automation of doubt in the process of receiving media content, and this automation of doubt could be a problem in itself.

Fortunately, in the end, it was not this small communicational event that prevented us from getting back into sport and getting our heads out of the digital environments in which we are immersed for a large part of our days.

#GenAI #automated_media #trust

entry.title: Measuring and defining informational vulnerability - EDMO Belux Lunch Lectures
entry.summary: I presented the current state of my research on how to define and measure "informational vulnerability", i.e. the risk for a person to be more susceptible to misinformation and disinformation.
entry.content:
Three weeks ago I had the chance to be the first guest of the EDMO Belux Lunch Lectures.

Edmo Belux is one of the EU-funded platforms that brings together actors from the field (fact-checkers, media and academics) to monitor and fight disinformation in Europe.

I presented the current state of my research on how to define and measure "informational vulnerability", i.e. the risk for a person to be more susceptible to misinformation and disinformation.

This presentation has been recorded and is available on the Edmo Belux Youtube account.

  • Link to the video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_whTK-Jtmrg
